newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi warns pilgrims to avoid politics.
newsitem.headline: Saudi warns pilgrims to avoid politics.

text.p: As thousands of Moslem pilgrims arrived by land, sea and air Saudi Arabia on Sunday renewed warnings to them to abide by its laws banning political activities.

An Interior Ministry statement said any of the two million Moslems expected to perform the "haj" pilgrimage in April found in possession of political material or carrying out political activity would be punished and deported.

The statement, carried by the official Saudi Press Agency, said violators of its ban on political material and activity ... "would be severely punished and will be subject to the laws of the kingdom... Any violators would be punished and deported."
The ministry has been issuing similar warnings for the past two months in the countdown to the haj, which is expected this year in the middle of April.

Saudi newspapers said on Sunday more than 370,000 pilgrims have so far arrived in the kingdom. Up to one million pilgrims from around the world perform the haj every year. They are joined by another one million who live in the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia, home to two of Islam's holiest shrines, is expected to announce the date for the start of haj next week.

The warnings are seen as directed at Iranian pilgrims, whose government says Moslems have the right to air their political grievances during the pilgrimage, mainly through rallies against Israel and the United States. Saudi Arabia says the haj is a purely religious affair and should not be politicised.
Saudi security forces clashed in 1987 with demonstrators in an Iranian-led rally in Mecca killing about 400 people, mainly Iranians. Iran boycotted the haj for the next three years.

Iran's ambassador to Saudi Arabia Mohammad Reza Nouri told a Saudi newspaper on Saturday that Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani is expected to make his first official visit to Saudi Arabia in April to perform haj.
Rafsanjani last travelled to Saudi at the start of the 1979 Iranian revolution on a personal visit to perform haj.
Iran's ties with Saudi Arabia have been tense since Iran's revolution, but Tehran has been trying to improve relations with Riyadh and other Gulf states.
Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said that his visit to Saudi Arabia earlier this month as part of a Gulf tour had opened up a new chapter in relations.
